# Overview

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy is a structured, time-limited, evidence-based form of psychotherapy grounded in the premise that thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are interconnected, so that changing unhelpful patterns of thinking can change how a person feels and acts. It was developed in the 1960s and has since accumulated one of the largest evidence bases of any psychological treatment. In practice, a course of therapy typically runs between twelve and twenty structured sessions, each with an agenda, a review of between-session practice, and collaborative goal setting. The therapist and the person work together to identify cognitive distortions such as catastrophizing, black-and-white thinking, overgeneralization, and mind reading, and then test those beliefs against the available evidence rather than accepting them at face value. Behavioral techniques, including activity scheduling, graded exposure, and behavioral experiments, complement the cognitive work by giving the person direct experiences that challenge unhelpful predictions. Because the approach is skills-based, a central aim is for the person to become their own therapist over time, carrying the methods forward after formal treatment ends. Reviews and meta-analyses consistently find it effective for depression and for most anxiety disorders, and it is frequently recommended as a first-line psychological treatment.

# Techniques

Common techniques include thought records, in which a person captures a situation, the automatic thoughts it triggered, the emotions that followed, and a more balanced alternative reading of the situation. Exposure hierarchies rank feared situations from least to most distressing so they can be approached gradually. Behavioral activation counters the withdrawal that maintains low mood by scheduling meaningful and rewarding activity.
